$comment: TEST FIXTURE -- the EXECUTOR's repository. Shaped after the Next.js product repo in zheref/nen#91's design (its two-step lint, its multi-package coverage, its unsupported archive/release/deploy), with this fixture's own placeholder workspace names: nothing here is any real project's identity. Not shipped; see ../../README.md. The `web` lane is the one stack this release runs end to end; `native` exists so the unsupported-verb, host, placeholder and cannot-assert refusals each have a lane to be proved against; `pages` is the one lane that CAN deploy, so that `--target` has somewhere to land -- `web`'s deploy is a SEAT on purpose, and the pair is what proves the order (a seat answers 4 whatever --target says; a runnable row asks for the destination).

web.why: The dependency install has been run. Nen ASSERTS it and never performs it: an install executes this project's own postinstall scripts. (The fixture carries deps/INSTALLED so this one is satisfied.)
Set by this project's own shell profile. Nen checks that the NAME is set and never reads, compares or prints the value.

native.why: Deliberately absent in this fixture: the unsatisfied-path refusal needs a lane to be proved against.
A kind this release cannot assert. It is reported as 'cannot assert' and refused -- never silently passed.

ui-test.why: Step 1 downloads a browser. It is part of the verb, not a precondition, because this project runs it every time.

lint.why: Two commands, in order. The second alone misses the repo-wide format check.

coverage.why: DELIBERATELY STALE, AND KEPT. This `report` key is the field zheref/nen#91's v4 §2.10 published for naming a coverage report; the shipped verb reads `artifacts` instead, and the schema preserves an unknown key rather than refusing it -- so a repository written against the published design has a perfectly reasonable-looking declaration that nen does not read. That is the exact case `nen shu coverage` must NAME rather than answer with 'declares no artifacts at all', and this row is what proves it does. It also states TWO of the three things at once: no `artifacts`, and a `report` that looks like it should serve as one.

run.why: The production serve, locally. Its env VALUE is declared here and must never appear in any output nen produces.

archive.unsupported: no packaging step exists; this lane ships as a web application.

release.unsupported: there is no package or store pipeline for this lane.

deploy.unsupported: no target is wired. Declare one under `targets` before nen will run this.

storybook.why: An UNKNOWN verb name, preserved rather than rejected -- the ecosystem's verbs are the repository's to name. `nen shu` has no such subcommand, so nothing here can reach it.

build.why: One argv element carries whitespace, so the dry run's quoting is proved against a declaration rather than a synthetic string.

release.why: Declared, and restricted to one platform under `hosts` -- the exit-3 refusal needs a verb that is real everywhere except the host.

test.why: A placeholder from the reference pack's own closed set, which this release cannot substitute -- the refusal is exit 2 naming it.

archive.unsupported: signing material is a human's, and nen never synthesises it.

dev.why: THE DEVICE-DESTINATION DEBUG BUILD, and the reason the `install` launch target below declares a `lane` at all: `defaultLane` is `web`, so a launch that did not say which lane it belongs to would run the simulator-shaped `dev` this repository iterates in. TWO artifacts, in this order, on purpose: `{artifact}` is the FIRST one, and the thing an installer puts on a handset is the SECOND -- which is what `project.launch.install.artifact` is for.

THE ONE LANE HERE THAT CARRIES A LAUNCH TARGET AND DOES NOT SIT AT THE REPOSITORY ROOT, which is the whole reason it exists. `artifacts` is repo-root-relative, as every declared path in this file is, while the `nested` target's after-steps are spawned in `native/` -- so `{artifact}` has to reach them as `../build/embedded/Placeholder.app`. Every other lane with a launch target has `cwd: "."`, where the two strings are identical, and that is exactly how the mismatch stayed invisible until a real declaration put a build one directory down. It declares no preconditions on purpose: this row's subject is a path, and an unmet precondition would refuse before the substitution was ever printed.

env.PLACEHOLDER_DEPLOY_CHANNEL: a declared value no output may carry

deploy.why: The one lane here that CAN deploy. Its argv names no destination -- that is what `targets` is for -- and its declared env VALUE exists so the rule that only NAMES are ever reported has a deploy to be proved against.

project.$targets: DELIBERATELY OUT OF BYTE ORDER in this file, so that a listing nen prints in byte order is provably sorted rather than provably echoed.

staging.why: Appends two arguments to the lane's declared deploy argv and requires one variable to be SET. Nen asserts the NAME and never reads the value.

production.why: Two required variables, declared out of byte order on purpose: the report sorts them.

preview.why: A NAME-ONLY target: it appends nothing and requires nothing, so `--target preview` runs the lane's declared argv exactly as written. Naming it is still mandatory -- nen never picks a destination.

provider-integration.unsupported: the push to the default branch IS the deploy here, through the hosting provider's git integration. There is no command line for nen to run, and inventing one that looked plausible is the failure this row exists to refuse.

project.$launch: The LAUNCH targets, a different block from `targets` and a different vocabulary: that one says where a build is SENT, this one says which DEVICE a local run lands on. Six rows, one per answer the resolver has to have -- a simulated device (no probe: the name IS the id), a probed device (the seam is scripted with its output), a target declared for the OTHER verb, a target with no command line at all, one that overrides BOTH the lane its verb is read from and the path {artifact} stands for, and one whose lane does not sit at the repository root.

sim.why: A SIMULATED device has no id to look up -- its name IS how the toolchain addresses it -- so this row resolves without spawning a probe at all.

handset.why: A REAL device: nen spawns the declared probe, searches its output for this exact name, and refuses at 5 listing what the probe DID offer when it is not there.

bench.why: Declared for 'run', so that naming it on 'dev' proves the verb check: the two are different builds, and nen carries a target across in neither direction.

farm.unsupported: the lab handsets are reached through a device farm's own web console. There is no command line for nen to run, and inventing one that looked plausible is the failure this row exists to refuse.

install.why: BOTH OVERRIDES AT ONCE, because in the field they arrive together. `lane` sends the verb to the `device` lane rather than to `defaultLane`'s `web` -- a device build is a different declared row from the one a developer iterates in -- and `artifact` names the SECOND of that row's two artifacts, because `{artifact}` is the first and the first is not what an installer takes.

nested.why: THE LANE WHOSE cwd IS NOT THE REPOSITORY ROOT. `embedded` runs in `native/`, so this after-step is spawned there while `project.verbs.embedded.dev.artifacts[0]` is stated -- like every declared path -- against the root. `{artifact}` therefore reaches the installer as `../build/embedded/Placeholder.app`, which is the same file the report's `artifacts:` line names as `build/embedded/Placeholder.app`: two roots, one file, and the report says both.
